content: Your doctor has prescribed nafcillin, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication will either be injected into a large muscle, such as your buttock or hip, or administered intravenously through a needle or catheter placed in your vein. The intravenous infusion will take 30 to 60 minutes and will be given four to six times a day. Nafcillin works by eliminating bacteria that cause infections, including pneumonia, meningitis, and infections of the urinary tract, skin, bones, joints, blood, and heart valves. In some cases, nafcillin may be prescribed for other uses. If you have questions about this, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Your healthcare provider may monitor the effectiveness of your treatment and check for side effects using laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Precautions Before Using Nafcillin: Inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to nafcillin, penicillin, cephalosporins, or any other drugs. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially antibiotics and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have or have ever had asthma, hay fever, or kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal diseases (especially colitis). Let your doctor know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking nafcillin, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and regularly check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape. Do not use Clinitest tablets, as nafcillin may cause false positive results. Administering Nafcillin: Before administering nafcillin, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or examine the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop your treatment prematurely, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this happens, contact your healthcare provider immediately to ensure your therapy continues without interruption. Side Effects: Minor Side Effects: Nafcillin may cause minor side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if these symptoms are severe or persistent: Upset stomach Diarrhea Severe Side Effects: If you experience any of the following symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately: Rash Itching Fever Chills Facial swelling Wheezing Difficulty breathing Unusual bleeding or bruising Dizziness Seizures Sore mouth or throat If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Storing Nafcillin: Your healthcare provider will likely give you a supply of nafcillin for several days at a time. If you are receiving nafcillin intravenously, you will likely be instructed to store it in the refrigerator or freezer. Take your next dose out of the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to warm to room temperature. If you are instructed to store additional nafcillin in the freezer, move a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day for the next day’s use. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving nafcillin intramuscularly, your healthcare provider will provide instructions on proper storage. Store the medication only as directed and ensure you understand the storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In Case of Emergency or Overdose: If you suspect an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Signs of Infection: If you are receiving nafcillin intravenously or under your skin, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection (an infection at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin).
